memory_update.text: New Hotspots currently clusters around AI infrastructure moving from chip scarcity to power, grid, memory, cooling, and policy chokepoints.
Large-load interconnection and cost-allocation policy should be tracked as a core regulation node for AI data-center buildout timing.
High-voltage transformers, switchgear, and cables are a cross-theme bottleneck spanning data centers, utilities, semiconductor fabs, renewables, and nuclear.
Advanced nuclear and firm-power supply chains should be decomposed into licensing, fuel, components, EPC, and grid integration rather than treated as a generic SMR theme.
HBM and advanced packaging remain a live AI compute bottleneck, with potential spillover into conventional DRAM and downstream electronics.
Before moving to Layer 1B or company ranking, verify supplier backlogs, qualification status, customer concentration, and market-pricing saturation using filings and current market data.

summary: Initial Serenity Layer 1A decomposition of the broad 'New Hotspots' theme. The strongest current hotspot cluster is not a single ticker story but a system-level collision between AI compute growth, power availability, grid interconnection policy, high-voltage equipment shortages, memory/HBM allocation, nuclear restart/advanced-reactor policy, and global logistics chokepoints. The priority for later layers is to separate durable bottlenecks from headline heat by mapping demand shocks to scarce nodes, qualification cycles, policy gates, and public-market exposures.

supply_chain_nodes.node: Large-load grid interconnection and transmission rules
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Track utilities, independent power producers, grid operators' exposed suppliers, transmission EPC firms, hyperscalers with contracted power, and data-center operators with secured interconnection. Pilot-universe links include AMZN, MSFT, GOOGL, META, CEG, NEE, PWR, ETN, GEV.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Do not start with one ticker. First classify headlines into six scarce layers: grid equipment, firm power/nuclear, AI memory and packaging, data-center thermal/electrical infrastructure, transmission/EPC services, and logistics/geopolitical risk hedges. Then map each layer to public assets by: 1) supplier concentration, 2) lead-time evidence, 3) customer qualification barriers, 4) backlog and pricing power, 5) policy exposure, 6) capex-cycle durability, and 7) falsification indicators such as hyperscaler capex cuts, faster-than-expected AI efficiency gains, regulatory pushback, commodity price reversal, or easing lead times.
supply_side_constraints: High-voltage transformers, switchgear, cables, and grid-supporting equipment have long lead times and limited qualified suppliers
Transmission interconnection queues and regional grid reliability rules can delay or cancel data-center projects even when compute hardware is available
Firm-power assets such as gas turbines, nuclear restarts, SMRs, geothermal, and large-scale storage face permitting, fuel, component, and EPC bottlenecks
HBM supply requires advanced DRAM capacity, TSV/stacking, CoWoS-like packaging, thermal engineering, and customer qualification
Critical minerals and metals such as copper, aluminum, silver, and rare earths are second-order constraints for servers, power systems, cooling, and grid buildouts
Maritime route disruption is shifting from single chokepoint risk toward network congestion and weather/geopolitical compounding risk
